{{nihongo|'''Minoru Tomita'''|冨田 稔|Tomita Minoru|extra=February 6, 1924 – October 9, 2015}} was a Japanese [[mathematician]] who made significant contributions to the theory of [[operator algebra]]s.

He became deaf at the age of two. He was described as a "very singular" personality.<ref>{{cite journal|author = Y K Leong|title=Interview with Huzihiro Araki: Mathematics and Physics, A Tale of Two Cultures|journal = Asia Pacific Mathematics Newsletter|url=http://www.asiapacific-mathnews.com/04/0402/0012_0018.pdf|year=2014|volume=4|number=2}}</ref>

Although he published relatively little, his 1967 manuscript on the theory of modular automorphisms of [[von Neumann algebra]]s was of major importance in the field. The manuscript was difficult to understand, but [[Masamichi Takesaki]] was able to revise it. In the summer of 1967 Takesaki communicated the results to [[Jacques Dixmier]],<ref>{{citation|url=http://math.edu.gunma-u.ac.jp/files/%E7%AB%B9%E5%B4%8E%E5%85%88%E7%94%9F%E3%81%94%E8%AC%9B%E6%BC%94%E4%BA%88%E7%A8%BF02.pdf|author = Masamichi Takesaki | year=2016|title=『数学を教えて学んだ事』 (Things I learned by teaching mathematics)}}</ref> and they became a major influence on the work of his student [[Alain Connes]] on the classification of type III factors.<ref>{{citation|url=http://www.nieuwarchief.nl/serie5/pdf/naw5-2010-11-4-250.pdf|title=The flashes of insight never came for free (interview with Alain Connes)|journal=Nieuw Archief voor Wiskunde|volume=5/11|issue=4|year=2010|pages=250–256|first1=Gunther|last1=Cornelissen|first2=Klaas|last2=Landsman|first3=Walter|last3=van Suijlekom}}</ref> The theory later became known as [[Tomita-Takesaki theory]].
